extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of advertising history; general educated public interested in fraudulent/rogue advertising practices
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts the recurring features, tactics, and warning signs of swindling advertisements (especially 19th-century newspaper ads and racing-tipster schemes) so readers can recognise fraud. Focuses on how adverts phrased guarantees, solicited payments, used vouchers/aliases, and otherwise manipulated victims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promise of absolute certainty / guaranteed wins
rubrics_metrics.description: Ad copy repeatedly claims events are 'absolute', 'undeniable', 'infallible', 'a foregone conclusion', or 'cannot possibly lose' (e.g., 'the most infallible and unerringly-successful winning guide', 'these undeniable and gold-producing morals', 'this race such an absolute foregone conclusion').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book highlights such categorical language as a primary red flag — advertisers framing speculative outcomes as moral/absolute certainties to entice speculative investors. Examples: Premier Racing Circular and Rawlings & Co. repeatedly used 'certainty' rhetoric to lure clients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requests for small prepaid items (stamps, stamped addressed envelope)
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisements ask readers to 'send six stamps and stamped addressed envelope for this week's number' or 'enclosing photograph and thirteen stamps' (e.g., horoscope, stage audition ads).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small prepaid items are used to extract immediate funds and create micro-payments that are hard to recover; they also screen and gather prospective victims. Repeatedly cited in multiple ads (racing circulars, horoscopes, acting offers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Offering to invest/back on clients' behalf (discretionary investment) and charging commission
rubrics_metrics.description: Adverts promise to 'undertake to obtain for them 6 to 4 for all cash sent' and charge a fee (e.g., 'five per cent commission charged on the winnings').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such offers concentrate control of stakes in the advertiser's hands, enabling them to bet against clients, misappropriate funds, or contrive outcomes. The text documents cases where firms took clients' money and backed the opposing horse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voucher-forcing scheme (send vouchers, then solicit stake money)
rubrics_metrics.description: Known as 'forcing the voucher': firms send apparent winning 'vouchers' (cheque-like slips) to victims and then request the stake money to be forwarded to realize the vouchers; if not accepted, victims are told to return vouchers immediately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book explains the detailed mechanics: victims receive winning vouchers that look genuine; the firm then pressures them to remit stake money or offers to 'correct' vouchers — a method to extract additional funds and delay/avoid payout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offering abnormally long/generous odds compared to market
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers 'offer far longer prices than could be obtained' and sometimes 'double the fair price' to entice clients (e.g., offering '6 to 4' or 'double the odds' when market was far shorter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mismatch signals fraud because credible bookmakers cannot sustainably offer such prices; the tactic entices those chasing big gains and sets up later default or cheating (e.g., backing the opposing horse themselves).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of fictitious or frequently changed business names / aliases
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisers frequently used fictitious names and altered them ('the names were, as a rule, fictitious, and often changed'), operating under aliases to avoid accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent name changes and fictitious proprietors are tactics to escape reputation damage and legal consequences; the text documents firms reappearing under new guises after exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circulars or letters giving plausible excuses for non-payment (delayed settlement)
rubrics_metrics.description: After sending vouchers/claims, firms reply with deferments: 'We regret to inform you that, in consequence of some of our important Accounts not having been settled at Epsom this week, we must unavoidably postpone the settlement.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These standardised stall tactics are used to buy time and avoid paying; the text reproduces such stock letters as part of the scam cycle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructed tables of past 'wins' showing small/close returns to imply legitimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Adverts provide tables of selections/wins that emphasize frequent small or near wins (selecting horses 'very close up', many seconds/thirds) and then show modest net balances after commissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such manufactured records are designed to look authoritative and plausible while masking that the returns are engineered to be low and believable. The book analyses sample tables used by Balliee & Walter and Rawlings & Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims of inside knowledge or secret influential coteries
rubrics_metrics.description: Copy asserts private information or influential backing: 'we have positive information that these horses cannot lose', 'This is a 'Woodyeates moral,' and all must be on', 'the influential coterie throws in for a fortune.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appealing to insider access or secret groups creates the illusion of privileged certainty; the text warns this is a rhetorical device to justify confident predictions and lure clients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solicitation of personal materials or sensitive personal data for bogus services
rubrics_metrics.description: Ads require photographs and personal details in exchange for promises (e.g., horoscope: 'age, height, colour of hair and eyes, together with 13 stamps' to receive 'a correct likeness of their future husband'; acting ads: 'enclosing photograph and thirteen stamps').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asking for photos/personal details plus payment is used to monetise vulnerability (young actors, marriage-curious individuals) and sometimes to perpetrate identity/romance fraud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale of spurious qualifications / 'promotion in absentia'
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisements offer to confer degrees and professional titles by correspondence: 'PROMOTION IN ABSENTIA.— Qualified surgeons, chemists, dentisits... may communicate... for a doctor's degree.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text flags these as scams producing worthless credentials that nonetheless allow recipients to claim titles; such schemes mix sham and real practitioners in society and harm public trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guaranteed returns framed as 'double the odds' or 'we will return double'
rubrics_metrics.description: Firms promise to 'return them double the odds' or otherwise guarantee to double clients' money as a favour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These explicit financial guarantees are unrealistic in zero-sum markets and indicate fraudulent intent; the narrative shows they were used to coax larger deposits and commitments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority- and virtue-signalling language (moral/gold-producing rhetoric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adverts employ moralizing and prosperity-laden phrases: 'moral certainty', 'gold-producing morals', 'promptitude, despatch, exactitude, and liberality will ever be our watchwords.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rhetorical veneer of respectability and virtue is used to mask dishonest operations; readers should treat grandiose moral claims as persuasive devices rather than evidence of legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeting victims' greed and promising easy wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: Schemes trade on 'greed and avarice' and target those seeking quick riches ('everyone should seize the opportunity of reaping the rich harvest', 'land a fortune over these genuine certainties').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book emphasises that such appeals to quick riches typically indicate scams; recognising the psychological hook (promises of effortless wealth) helps detect fraudulent adverts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recruitment/engagement offers that ask for payment from applicants
rubrics_metrics.description: Stage/acting ads solicit application materials plus stamps/payments: 'WANTED... Totallly inexperienced persons may apply — Communicate by letter only, enclosing photograph and thirteen stamps.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pattern of requiring payment from applicants for promised employment is a frequent swindle against vulnerable job-seekers; treating any paid-application claim with scepticism is recommended.
